messages.content: You are a staff engineer at Relay, a B2B invoicing SaaS. Answer using only the documents the user provides; cite documents and sections by their identifiers.

# Doc A — Session Tokens v2 proposal (Marta K., March 12)

## A.1 Summary

Relay's web and mobile clients authenticate against opaque session tokens stored
in the shared Redis session cluster (sessions-prod). Every authenticated request
costs one Redis round trip to resolve the token to a user id, an org id, and a
role set. At current traffic (about 9,400 authenticated requests per second at
peak) the session cluster is the single hottest dependency in the stack, and it
is also the least loved: it runs an old Redis 5 build, its failover has paged us
four times this year, and every new region we open needs a cross-region session
replication story we do not really have. This proposal replaces the opaque
tokens with stateless signed JWTs so that request authentication becomes a local
signature check with no network hop.

## A.2 Current state

A session is created at login and written to Redis with the key sess:<token>.
The TTL on the session is 30 days; users effectively stay logged in for a month
and the mobile team has repeatedly asked us not to shorten this because a login
on mobile is a high-friction event (password manager round trip, sometimes SMS
2FA). The 30-day figure matters for sizing: the cluster currently holds about
41 million live sessions at roughly 600 bytes each. There is no refresh
mechanism anywhere in the stack today: a session lives its 30 days and then the
client re-authenticates from scratch.

## A.3 Client constraints

The web client can adopt whatever we ship, since we control the deploy. The
mobile app is the binding constraint. The mobile client cannot refresh tokens:
it has no background scheduler for credential renewal, no silent re-auth path,
and the keychain wrapper it uses only supports write-once storage of a single
credential blob. When its session expires, the app throws the user back to the
login screen. This is confirmed by the mobile team's January comment on
PLAT-641 and it is why any design that depends on short-lived credentials plus
refresh is a non-starter for us: we would be logging every mobile user out every
few minutes. Whatever we ship, the mobile credential must live as long as the
session does today.

## A.4 Proposed design

Issue a JWT at login signed with an asymmetric key (ES256), carrying user id,
org id, role hash, and an exp claim set to 30 days to match the session
lifetime the clients already assume. Services verify the signature locally
against a published JWKS document; no Redis on the hot path. Logout deletes the
client-side token. Because verification is stateless, a stolen token remains
valid until exp; we accept this because the current opaque tokens are already
bearer credentials, and 30 days is the lifetime users already live with.

## A.5 Redis stays as a fallback

We keep sessions-prod as a fallback store: tokens minted before the cutover
keep resolving through Redis until they age out, and if the JWKS distribution
has an incident we can fail back to opaque tokens with a config flip. Retiring
the cluster is explicitly out of scope for this proposal; plan on it staying
for at least another year.

## A.6 Rollout

Dual-issue for one release (JWT plus legacy token), verify JWTs in the gateway
behind a flag, flip the flag org by org, remove legacy issuance in Q4. Open
questions: key rotation cadence for the signing key, and whether the role hash
belongs in the token at all given role edits currently take effect on the next
Redis read.

## A.7 Alternatives considered

Paseto instead of JWT: strictly nicer cryptographic hygiene, but every gateway
library we run already verifies JWTs and none speaks Paseto; not worth the
integration tax for a format change with the same trust model. Sticky sessions
at the load balancer to keep Redis lookups region-local: rejected because it
couples session validity to LB affinity and breaks the moment a client roams
between regions, which our mobile traffic does constantly. A per-service
session cache in front of Redis: this is what three teams have already built
independently, with three different TTLs and three different invalidation bugs;
the whole point of this proposal is to delete that pattern, not bless it. Doing
nothing and upgrading sessions-prod to Redis 7 in place: does not remove the
network hop, does not solve cross-region, and keeps us on the hook for a
cluster nobody wants to own.

# Doc B — Platform security review of Session Tokens v2 (Security guild, May 28)

Scope: Doc A as written, reviewed against the credential-handling standard
(SEC-STD-4) and the incident history of the last two years, including INC-3310
(a session token exfiltrated from a browser extension and replayed for 11 days
before detection). Findings are numbered; MUST findings block the design.

## SR-1 (MUST) — Revocation latency

Any credential accepted by production services must be revocable within 60
seconds of a logout, a password change, or a compromise report. Doc A section
A.4 explicitly accepts that a stolen JWT stays valid until exp. With a 30-day
exp this recreates INC-3310 with a longer replay window and no kill switch. A
pure stateless design cannot satisfy this finding; some server-side check is
required on the validation path, however cheap.

## SR-2 (MUST) — Access credential lifetime

Under SEC-STD-4 section 7, a bearer credential presented on every request (an
access token) may live at most 15 minutes. Long-lived state, if any, must be a
separate credential that is exchanged, not presented, on the request path. The
30-day exp in Doc A A.4 exceeds the standard by three orders of magnitude and
was the review's first blocking comment.

## SR-3 (MUST) — No long-lived bearer blobs on mobile

The write-once keychain wrapper described in Doc A A.3 stores one opaque blob
for the life of the install. Whatever we ship must tolerate that blob being
extracted once: a 30-day all-powerful bearer token does not.

## SR-4 (SHOULD) — Denylist is an acceptable revocation mechanism

A signed access token checked against a small in-memory denylist of revoked
token ids (jti), replicated to every gateway within seconds, satisfies SR-1
while keeping validation local in the common case. The denylist stays bounded
because it only has to hold revocations younger than the access-token TTL,
which is another reason SR-2's 15-minute cap matters: at 15 minutes the
denylist is a few thousand entries; at 30 days it would be the Redis cluster
again under a different name.

## SR-5 (MUST) — Refresh tokens must rotate

If the design introduces refresh tokens, each refresh token is single-use: the
exchange endpoint returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, and
reuse of an invalidated token revokes the whole session family (this is the
standard rotation-with-reuse-detection scheme). This is what turns "the mobile
blob was extracted once" from a 30-day incident into a bounded one.

## SR-6 (constraint inherited from Doc A) — Mobile cannot refresh

We accept Doc A A.3's statement that the mobile client has no refresh path and
write-once credential storage. Given SR-2 and SR-5, that leaves only one
compliant option for mobile: keep mobile on server-side opaque sessions
(Redis), and ship short-lived JWTs for web only. The review recommends exactly
that split, with the explicit note that it is ugly, doubles the auth code
paths, and should be revisited the moment the mobile constraint moves.

# Doc C — Mobile client capabilities audit (Deniz A., July 30)

This audit was commissioned after the May security review to pin down what the
mobile app can actually do in 2026, because several platform documents were
found to be citing mobile constraints from 2023. Method: read the current
mobile auth module (mobile-core/auth, commit 41c9d2e), interviewed the two
mobile leads, and pulled adoption numbers from the release dashboard on
July 28.

## C.1 App landscape

Two binaries (iOS, Android) built from one React Native codebase with a shared
native auth module. Release train is weekly; forced-upgrade floor is currently
5.9, set in April. Version adoption on July 28: 6.6 at 31.4%, 6.5 at 40.1%,
6.4 at 22.7%, everything older 5.8%.

## C.2 Network stack

All API traffic goes through a single retry-aware fetch wrapper
(mobile-core/net). Certificate pinning since 5.2. The wrapper has an
interceptor chain; the auth interceptor is registered first and sees every 401
before any caller does. This matters below.

## C.3 Credential storage

The write-once keychain wrapper that older platform docs describe was replaced
in release 6.0 (shipped February) by SecureCredentialStore, which supports
atomic read-modify-write of a structured record (iOS Keychain with
kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock, Android EncryptedSharedPreferences backed
by StrongBox where available). The store holds a record per environment:
{ access_token, refresh_token, issued_at, rotation_counter }.

## C.4 Background execution

There is still no reliable background scheduler on iOS, and the audit found
none is needed: renewal is entirely reactive (see C.7). The January PLAT-641
comment saying the app "cannot refresh tokens" described the pre-6.0 module
and was accurate when written; it has been overtaken by events.

## C.5 Session lifetime as actually configured

The 30-day session figure quoted in several documents comes from the marketing
site's visitor cookie, not from the product. The API session TTL is set by
SESSION_TTL_HOURS in api-config/prod.yaml and has been 24 (one day) since the
INC-3310 remediation last November. The mobile app has therefore been living
with daily credential expiry for eight months. User-visible re-login prompts
did not spike when that change shipped, for the reason described in C.7.

## C.6 Dependency note: sessions-prod

While tracing the login path we confirmed with the platform team that the
shared Redis session cluster (sessions-prod) is scheduled for decommission at
the end of Q1 next year under mandate PLAT-772 (the Redis 5 fleet is being
retired; nothing gets a new lease on it). Any design that keeps sessions-prod
as a long-term fallback needs to either take over ownership of a replacement
cluster or drop the dependency. The platform team was surprised to hear a
proposal was planning to keep it "for at least another year."

## C.7 Token handling since 6.4

Release 6.4 (May) shipped full reactive token renewal, and this is the
audit's central finding. The auth interceptor performs silent refresh on 401:
when any API call returns 401 with error code token_expired, the interceptor
holds the failed request, calls POST /auth/refresh with the stored refresh
token, writes the new pair to SecureCredentialStore under a mutex (single
flight; concurrent 401s wait on the same renewal), and replays the held
request with the new access token. Refresh tokens are one-time-use rotating
tokens: every successful refresh returns a new refresh token and increments
rotation_counter, and the server invalidates the old one. Reuse detection on
the server side revokes the session family and forces re-login. The mechanism
has been exercised in production by the 24-hour TTL since May. Combined
adoption of 6.4 and later was 94.2% on July 28, and the forced-upgrade floor
reaches 6.4 in September under the standard two-release policy, taking that to
100% before any Q4 cutover.

## C.8 What the app cannot do

For completeness: no WebAuthn/passkey support yet (targeted at 7.x), no DPoP
or other proof-of-possession (the SDK we would need is still in beta), and
offline mode keeps read-only cached data for 72 hours regardless of token
state. Nothing in Q4 scope depends on these.

## C.9 Audit recommendations

First, platform documents that cite mobile constraints should cite this audit
by section rather than PLAT-641, which describes a module that no longer
exists. Second, any Q4 token design should treat the mobile client as a fully
capable OAuth-style client: short-lived access token, rotating refresh token,
reactive renewal — that is what is deployed and exercised today, not an
aspiration. Third, the sessions-prod decommission (C.6) is a hard external
deadline that at least one in-flight proposal appears unaware of; whoever owns
the token work should own the dependency removal too, because after Q1 there
is nothing to fall back to. Fourth, the forced-upgrade floor should be raised
to 6.4 in September as already planned; the 5.8% of traffic below 6.4 is the
only cohort that would still behave the way the March proposal assumes, and it
rounds to zero before cutover.

You have the three documents above: Doc A (March proposal), Doc B (May
security review), Doc C (July mobile capabilities audit). They disagree, and
the later documents correct the earlier ones in places that change the
conclusion. Write the Q4 token architecture recommendation for the platform
leads. Requirements:

1. The recommended architecture, concretely: what credential each client holds,
   lifetimes, and how logout/compromise revocation works. Address each MUST
   finding in Doc B by its SR number and name the mechanism that satisfies it.
2. A section titled "Corrections" listing every claim in Doc A or Doc B that
   Doc C invalidates. For each, cite the claim (document and section), cite the
   Doc C section that overrides it, and for the mobile-refresh claim name the
   exact client release that changed the picture and its combined adoption
   figure from the audit.
3. The access-token lifetime you would ship, and why.
4. What this means for the sessions-prod Redis cluster, given C.6.

Base every statement on the documents; do not invent capabilities.

notes: About 2,700 words across three documents that contradict each other; the correct recommendation depends on audit findings buried in Doc C (6.4 silent refresh, 94.2% adoption, Redis decommission) that invalidate the premises of Docs A and B. Band 3 synthesis across a large input; band 3 is always frontier.

messages.content: You take meeting minutes that record decisions and ownership accurately, including decisions that changed during the meeting.

Meeting: Analytics storage decision — platform sync
Date: Tuesday, 10:00-11:00
Present: Rachel (eng manager, chair), Dana (data eng), Marcus (backend), Priya (SRE). Tom (finance BP) joins late.

[10:01] Rachel: Okay, goal for the hour: pick a home for product analytics events. Current state, for the record: everything lands in the main Postgres instance, events table, 1.9 billion rows, and the nightly rollup job now takes six hours.

[10:02] Dana: And growing. We ingest about 11 million events a day now, up from 7 in March. The events table is 60% of the database by size, and the rollup job finished at 9:40 this morning. It's supposed to feed the 8am dashboards.

[10:03] Marcus: The app queries are fine, to be clear. It's only the analytical scans that hurt. OLTP p99 is still 12ms except while the rollup runs — then it triples.

[10:04] Priya: From my side: the instance is at 71% disk, and vacuum on the events table takes most of Sunday. Whatever we choose, I want the events table out of the primary within two quarters. I've been saying this since the March incident where the rollup and a schema migration collided and we served stale dashboards for a day and a half.

[10:04] Rachel: Fair, and for the minutes: the requirement is events off the primary by end of Q1, owned by this group, whatever storage we pick. That part is not up for debate today, only the destination is.

[10:05] Rachel: Options on the table from Dana's doc: one, ClickHouse Cloud; two, keep Postgres but partition the events table and move it to its own instance; three, something like Snowflake, which we scoped out last year on cost — the quote came back at roughly four times the ClickHouse number for our shape of workload, so it stays scoped out unless someone objects. Hearing none. Dana, run us through it.

[10:06] Dana: The doc's short version. ClickHouse: purpose-built for this, our rollup queries run 40 to 200 times faster in my benchmark — I loaded a 90-day sample, the six-hour rollup finishes in four minutes. Compression is about 8x better than what we see in Postgres, so storage roughly stops being a topic. Downsides: new system to operate, new query dialect for anything that touches it, and the app can't join events against app tables anymore — the two datasets live in different places.

[10:08] Marcus: How much of our reporting SQL survives the dialect change?

[10:09] Dana: Most SELECTs port with small edits. The window-function-heavy stuff needs rewriting, that's maybe a dozen queries. The bigger lift is ingestion: we'd move from inserting into Postgres to batching into ClickHouse, which is where the two-ish months of my time in the doc goes.

[10:10] Priya: Managed ClickHouse Cloud, or self-hosted?

[10:11] Dana: The doc assumes ClickHouse Cloud. Self-hosting is doable but it's a stateful cluster with its own replication and upgrade story — that's real SRE surface we don't have today.

[10:12] Priya: Agreed, if we go ClickHouse I want the managed one. I have no appetite for babysitting a third stateful system alongside Postgres and Redis.

[10:13] Rachel: Cost of managed?

[10:14] Dana: Rough quote from their calculator with our volume: about $5,800 a month at today's ingest, growing with volume. Postgres option two is roughly $1,900 a month for a dedicated replica-sized instance, but it doesn't fix the query speed, just isolates the pain.

[10:15] Marcus: Honestly the speed numbers are hard to argue with. Six hours to four minutes changes what the analytics team can even ask. My only hesitation is the join problem — billing reconciliation and the fraud checks both join events to app tables today, and splitting the data means those become two-source jobs forever.

[10:16] Rachel: Provisionally I agree ClickHouse looks like the answer. Let's stress-test the Postgres option so we're honest. Marcus, steelman it.

[10:17] Marcus: Fine. Option two: declarative partitioning on the events table by month with pg_partman, move it to its own instance, and rebuild the rollup as incremental — process only yesterday's partition instead of scanning everything. The six hours isn't inherent; most of it is re-scanning history we've already rolled up. Incremental gets us to maybe 20 minutes, not 4, but 20 minutes at 6am is fine. All existing SQL keeps working, all joins keep working, zero new operational surface, and Priya gets the table off the primary either way.

[10:19] Dana: The incremental rewrite isn't free either — the rollup job has ten years of accreted logic. Call it three or four weeks of my time, and we're still on a row store; ad-hoc exploration over the full history stays slow. The analytics team's actual complaint isn't the 8am dashboards, it's that any new question over more than 90 days takes 20 minutes to answer.

[10:20] Rachel: That's a fair distinction — dashboards versus exploration. ClickHouse fixes both, Postgres fixes only the first.

[10:21] Priya: Operationally I mildly prefer option two because it's boring, but managed ClickHouse addresses most of my concern. I can live with either. My hard requirement is just: events off the primary by end of Q1.

[10:22] Rachel: Noted. So, tentative direction: ClickHouse Cloud, Dana owns the migration plan, Marcus reviews the query ports. Dana, what's the timeline look like?

[10:23] Dana: Contract signed by end of month, dual-write from November, backfill the history over two weekends, cut the dashboards over in January, decommission the events table in February.

[10:24] Marcus: One flag for the plan: billing reconciliation joins events against invoices today, in SQL. If events move out, that job needs to pull from two sources. Not a blocker, but it's a week of work nobody scoped.

[10:25] Dana: Fair, I'll add it to the doc.

[10:26] Rachel: Okay. Unless finance surprises us, I think we have a direction. Tom said he'd try to join the last twenty minutes — let's use the gap to settle the rollout details.

[10:27] Dana: For dual-write, I want a feature flag per event type. We turn on the noisy ones first — page views, clicks — and keep checkout events on Postgres until we trust the pipeline.

[10:29] Marcus: And an idempotency key on the batcher, or dual-write will double-count on retries. The event UUID works.

[10:31] Priya: Alerting: I want lag between the two stores as a first-class metric from day one of dual-write, not after the first incident.

[10:33] Rachel: Good. Also — analytics team training on the dialect. Dana, can your team run a lunch-and-learn in November?

[10:34] Dana: Sure, two sessions, one for the SQL crowd, one for the dashboard builders.

[10:36] Marcus: While we wait for Tom — Dana, what happens to the raw event archive in S3? Do we keep writing it?

[10:37] Dana: Yes, unchanged. It's our replay source if any store gets corrupted, ClickHouse or not. It costs about $400 a month in Glacier tiers and I'd like to keep it forever; it has saved us twice.

[10:38] Rachel: Agreed, the archive is out of scope today. One more while we wait — Priya, anything from the analytics team survey worth putting on the record?

[10:39] Priya: Two things. Forty-one respondents: the top complaint was exploration speed, like Dana said — 28 people ranked it first. Second was dashboard freshness, 9 people. Nobody complained about the query language, which mildly undercuts my dialect worry. And three teams admitted to exporting CSVs to laptops to get around slow queries, which is its own governance problem whatever we pick.

[10:40] Rachel: Noted, and the CSV thing goes on the security backlog regardless of today's outcome.

[10:41] Tom: (joins) Sorry — board prep ran over. Where did you land?

[10:42] Rachel: Tentatively: ClickHouse Cloud for analytics events. Roughly $5,800 a month at current volume, growing with ingest, plus about two months of Dana's time for migration. Postgres partitioning was the runner-up at about $1,900 a month but it only fixes the dashboards, not exploration.

[10:43] Tom: Ah. Okay, I have to be the bearer of bad news then, because this is exactly what I came to flag. As of the September board meeting there's a freeze on new vendor contracts above $2,000 a month through the end of the fiscal year — that's June for us. Anything above that needs CFO sign-off, and I can tell you the two requests that have gone up since the freeze both came back no. A new $70k-a-year data vendor is not getting approved this year. I'm sorry, I know that upends things.

[10:45] Rachel: That... substantially changes the meeting. Is there any carve-out? The engineering-tools budget?

[10:46] Tom: The freeze is on new vendor contracts, full stop. Expanding an existing contract is treated differently — that's why the AWS bill growing doesn't need sign-off. Self-hosted on our existing AWS account would technically be inside the freeze rules, for what it's worth.

[10:47] Priya: I want it on the record that self-hosted ClickHouse is the one option I object to. A stateful analytics cluster we operate ourselves is a bigger operational risk than the problem we're solving. I'd rather stay on Postgres.

[10:48] Dana: And I'll admit the honest version of self-hosting: with hiring frozen too, the operational load lands on me and Priya. The benchmark was fun; running ZooKeeper — or Keeper — in anger is not.

[10:49] Rachel: Okay. Let me re-frame. Given the freeze: option two was designed for exactly this. Marcus, your 10:17 steelman becomes the plan. Partitioned events table on a dedicated instance — that's AWS spend on the existing contract, Tom, correct?

[10:50] Tom: Correct, that's fine under the freeze.

[10:51] Rachel: Then here's what I propose we actually decide today. One: we go with Postgres partitioning — pg_partman, monthly partitions, dedicated instance — and the incremental rollup rewrite. Marcus owns that, targeting events off the primary by end of Q1, which also meets Priya's requirement. Two: the ClickHouse direction is deferred, not dead — Dana runs a low-stakes self-hosted spike on a single node, on existing hardware, replaying the S3 archive, so we walk into the vendor conversation next fiscal year with real numbers. Cap it at 15% of Dana's time. Three: we revisit the vendor decision when the freeze lifts in June, with Tom in the room from the start this time.

[10:53] Dana: I can live with that. The spike answers the two things the benchmark didn't: ingestion shape and operational feel. To be clear though, the spike is throwaway — nothing production points at it.

[10:54] Marcus: Taking the partitioning work. I'll want Priya for the instance provisioning and the cutover window.

[10:54] Priya: Fine. I'll also set up the disk and vacuum alerts on the new instance before data moves, not after.

[10:55] Tom: And send me the projected AWS delta for the dedicated instance — under the freeze I don't need to approve it, but I want it in the forecast.

[10:56] Rachel: Deal. Recap of owners before we close: Marcus — partition migration plan and incremental rollup, draft by next Friday. Priya — instance provisioning plan and alerting. Dana — spike write-up by end of November, plus the November lunch-and-learns are cancelled... no, wait, those were for the ClickHouse dialect. Cancelled. Instead, Dana documents the query patterns that stay slow so the June conversation has evidence. Tom — flag the freeze status to us if anything changes before June. I'll update the roadmap and tell the analytics team why exploration stays slow for now. Thanks everyone — good meeting, honest meeting.

[10:58] (meeting ends)

messages.content: You are the database reliability lead. Produce complete, actionable operational documents; never hand-wave a required section.

We need a written migration plan to partition our orders table. Context:

- PostgreSQL 15 on RDS (db.r6g.4xlarge, one primary, two read replicas).
- Table `orders`: 220M rows, 410 GB with indexes, append-heavy, ~4,000
  writes/min at peak (14:00-20:00 UTC), read by the storefront (point lookups
  by id and by customer_id) and by a nightly finance export (full month scans).
- Compliance requires 7 years of order history online; months older than 24
  months are read only by the finance export.
- Allowed downtime: one maintenance window per month, Sunday 04:00-04:10 UTC
  (10 minutes, hard limit — checkout keeps running against a queue-and-replay
  buffer that holds at most 10 minutes of writes).
- Target: native declarative partitioning by month on `created_at`, managed
  with pg_partman, old months eventually moved to cheaper storage via
  tablespaces. The storefront must not see error-rate or latency regressions.

Write the plan as a single document with EXACTLY these seven numbered
sections, each substantive (no one-line sections):

1. Pre-migration checklist — everything verified before any change, including
   how each item is checked.
2. Migration steps — ordered, with the actual SQL/commands, and which steps
   run inside vs outside the 10-minute window. If you use a
   create-new-partitioned-table-and-backfill approach, show the trigger or
   dual-write mechanics and the batched backfill with its batch size and
   throttle.
3. Rollback plan — how we abort at each phase boundary, and the last phase
   at which rollback is still possible without data loss.
4. Risk table — a markdown table with columns Risk | Likelihood | Impact |
   Mitigation, at least six rows, covering at minimum: replica lag during
   backfill, the 10-minute window overrunning, the finance export breaking on
   partition pruning, and queue-and-replay buffer overflow.
5. Timeline — week-by-week schedule with the specific maintenance windows
   used and what happens in each.
6. Verification queries — the SQL run after each phase to prove row counts,
   constraint validity, and partition routing are correct.
7. Stakeholder communication — who is told what, when: storefront team,
   finance, support, and the exec summary line.

All seven sections are required. Omitting or merging sections fails the task.

notes: A seven-part migration plan against hard operational constraints (10-minute window, compliance retention, live checkout) where every section must be produced and internally consistent. Large-scope, correctness-critical ops planning: band 3, always frontier.

messages.content: You are the API design lead for a billing platform. Write precise, complete API design documents in markdown.

Design the public webhook-subscriptions API for our billing platform (REST,
JSON). Deliver a design document covering ALL of the following numbered
requirements — every one must appear:

1. Resource model and endpoints: subscriptions as a resource under
   /v1/webhook_subscriptions with create, get, list, update, delete, plus a
   test-delivery endpoint. Show the method and path for each.
2. List pagination: cursor-based, with `cursor` and `limit` query parameters
   and a `next_cursor` field in the response. State the default and maximum
   `limit`.
3. Error catalog: a table of every error the API returns, covering at
   minimum HTTP 400, 401, 404, 409, 422, and 429, each with a stable
   machine-readable `code` string and when it occurs.
4. Idempotency: creates and updates accept an `Idempotency-Key` header;
   specify the retention window and what happens on key reuse with a
   different body.
5. Delivery semantics: retry schedule with exponential backoff (give the
   actual schedule), delivery ordering guarantees (or the lack of them), and
   when a subscription is auto-disabled.
6. Security: each delivery is signed with an HMAC-SHA256 signature in the
   `X-Relay-Signature` header; document the exact string-to-sign, the
   timestamp element that prevents replay, and the verification steps a
   consumer follows.
7. Versioning: how the event payload schema is versioned and how a consumer
   pins and migrates versions; include one worked example of a create request
   and its response body (full JSON), showing the version field.

Number your sections 1-7 to match. A design missing any requirement is

- Three shards (cache-a, cache-b, cache-c), each one primary and two
  replicas, coordinated by Redis Sentinel (three sentinel nodes:
  sentinel-1..3, quorum 2).

  disconnect. Sessions are NOT in this cluster (they moved out last year);

  identity, and replication lag; the alert CacheHitRateLow fires below 80%.

  a failover promotes a stale replica and recently-written keys revert —
  acceptable for cache data but it must be stated, and lag must be checked
  first.

  lead; the vendor support contract covers Sentinel bugs only.

others: "## Overview", "## Preconditions", "## Failover procedure",
"## Validation", "## Rollback", "## Escalation". Under Preconditions include
